name: The Oz Bar
description: The Oz Bar has traded from this corner of Candlemaker Row, just off the Grassmarket, since 1997, giving Edinburgh's Australian community and expats a proper home-away-from-home. Its interior leans hard into the theme: corrugated-iron cladding, an outback-shed feel, and shelves cluttered with Australian curios, football jumpers and beach-postcard kitsch, all under a genuinely ramshackle tin awning. It has outlasted most of the other Australian-themed bars that have come and gone in the city over the years, largely on the strength of screening Aussie Rules and rugby league fixtures live and keeping a menu of proper Australian pub food and beer on tap.
interesting_fact: Candlemaker Row itself takes its name from the candlemakers' guild that worked this stretch of the Old Town from the 17th century, making the Oz Bar's very Australian theme sit on one of the more purely Scottish trade-guild streets in the city.
source_notes: History (est. 1997, Australian theme, longevity) drawn from Yelp/Useyourlocal/brewmook reviews. Google Places confirms address/coordinates at 33 Candlemaker Row. Leg assigned by geography (matches existing leg-10 Victoria Street/George IV Bridge POIs).

name: West Bow Well
description: This carved stone wellhead at the foot of Victoria Street was erected in 1674 by master mason Robert Mylne as Edinburgh's very first public wellhead, part of the city's earliest piped water supply instigated by Lord Provost Sir Andrew Ramsay. Water was carried down from reservoirs fed by springs in the Pentland Hills, and the West Bow Well became the first stop for the city's water caddies - workers who queued here to fill their kegs before hauling water door to door through the tenements above the Grassmarket. Its square-plan structure carries a semi-circular drinking basin on one face beneath a 19th-century Edinburgh coat of arms, with a smaller ornamental basin and heraldic panel on its other sides.
interesting_fact: The well stopped supplying water in the early 19th century once piped plumbing reached individual buildings, but a small iron door on it still carries its original inscription: 'The West-Bow Well erected by The Town Council 1674. Repaired and Altered by Richardson Brothers Merchants West Bow 1861.'
source_notes: History from Canmore/trove.scot and Art UK entries on West Bow Well. Google Places lists it as 'Bow Well' at 94/1 W Bow. Leg assigned by geography (foot of Victoria Street, matches existing leg-10 POIs).

name: Museum Context
description: This three-floor shop on Victoria Street is one of the city's best-known officially licensed Harry Potter retailers, packed with wands, house scarves, robes and collectibles across a warren of small rooms. The building itself has a history that suits its current trade: for more than 130 years it housed Robert Cresser's brush shop, a Victorian ironmonger-style store selling brooms, brushes and household wares from floor-to-ceiling wooden fittings and dusty stock boxes. That original Victorian interior survives largely intact behind the modern merchandise, and its cluttered, old-fashioned character is often cited by visitors and Potter fans as an uncanny match for Ollivanders wand shop in Diagon Alley.
interesting_fact: The shop's top floor has a free photo spot with props and house robes, including a mirror etched with the 'Chamber of Secrets' inscription - a nod to the wider theory, encouraged by J.K. Rowling having written much of the early books nearby, that this curving street inspired Diagon Alley itself.
source_notes: Building history (Robert Cresser Brush Shop, 130+ years, Ollivanders comparison) from thirdeyetraveller.com and geekytourist.com. Google Places confirms 40 Victoria Street. Content kept distinct from the existing Victoria Street POI, which already covers the street's own Diagon Alley theory in general terms.

name: The Enchanted Galaxy
description: The Enchanted Galaxy sits at the top of Victoria Street and, like its rival Museum Context further down the hill, trades on the street's Diagon Alley reputation - but with a name that took three attempts to land. Run by the Gold brothers, the shop originally opened as 'The Boy Wizard', a name Warner Bros objected to for trading too directly on Harry Potter trademarks. A rebrand to 'The Great Wizard' ran into the same problem, and the owners eventually settled on 'The Enchanted Galaxy', blending magical and sci-fi themes broadly enough to sidestep further disputes while still selling largely Potter-themed merchandise alongside Star Wars, Marvel and other franchise collectibles.
interesting_fact: Where Museum Context leans into cramped, cluttered Victorian atmosphere, The Enchanted Galaxy goes the opposite way - reviewers have compared its clean, brightly lit layout to 'an Apple Store', making the two competing shops, barely 150 metres apart, a study in opposite ways of selling the same theme.
source_notes: Name-change history (Boy Wizard -> Great Wizard -> Enchanted Galaxy, Warner Bros trademark pressure, Gold brothers ownership) from pottertour.co.uk. Google Places confirms 1 Victoria Street.

name: Bertie's Proper Fish & Chips
description: Bertie's occupies a genuinely surprising building for a chip shop: a former church. The site had stood empty for a decade, ever since a serious fire gutted its previous occupant, an Indian restaurant called Khushi's, when the Vittoria Group - the Crolla family's Edinburgh restaurant business - spent £3 million converting the old St John's church into a three-floor, 300-seat fish and chip restaurant that opened in 2018. The name honours Alberto 'Bertie' Crolla, the group's founder, and the restaurant now sits just a few streets from its sister restaurant Landy's on North Bridge, both built on the same family's decades-long fish-and-chip tradition in the city.
interesting_fact: The building's church origins are still legible in its bones - tall arched windows and a soaring, three-storey-high interior - giving diners eating double-cooked chips and battered haddock a dining room shaped like a nave.
source_notes: History (former St John's church, Khushi's fire, £3M Vittoria Group conversion, 2018 opening, Bertie=Alberto Crolla) from champagne-tastes.com and snackmag.co.uk. Google Places confirms 9 Victoria Street. Cross-referenced against Landy's Fish and Chips (already drafted, leg 5) - same Vittoria Group/Crolla family, noted as a connection rather than a duplicate.

name: Finnegan's Wake
description: Finnegan's Wake has been Victoria Street's Irish pub since 1994, when it took over the premises of a live-music venue called the Preservation Hall and kept the tradition of nightly bands going. Its interior is built around a large circular bar with small wood-panelled booths around the edge and a raised corner stage where bands still play live Irish music most nights, alongside sport on the screens and Guinness on tap. Its name borrows directly from James Joyce's famously dense, unfinished-feeling final novel, itself named after an old Irish-American comic ballad about a hod-carrier who wakes up mid-funeral - a fittingly playful, slightly literary joke for a pub sitting almost next door to Bertie's converted church.
interesting_fact: The pub sits at 9B Victoria Street, immediately beside Bertie's Fish & Chips at number 9 - two very different Irish/British institutions sharing practically the same doorway on the street's lower curve.
source_notes: History (1994 opening, former Preservation Hall site, live music tradition) from edinburghguide.com and bestpubs.co.uk. Google Places confirms 9B Victoria Street.

name: John Kay's Shop
description: This small green-fronted shop at the top of Victoria Street sells prints, postcards and Scottish artworks and mementos, and takes its name from John Kay (1742-1826), one of Edinburgh's most important social chroniclers. Kay worked as a barber in the Old Town before his sketching hobby overtook his trade; by 1785 he had given up cutting hair to run a print shop of his own in Parliament Close, where he produced and sold etched caricatures of the city's great and ordinary figures alike. Over nearly 900 etchings between 1785 and 1820, he documented everyone from Enlightenment intellectuals to street vendors, most sketched from nothing more than a passing glance, leaving behind one of the richest visual records of Georgian Edinburgh life.
interesting_fact: The modern shop is a separate business (incorporated in 2017) rather than a surviving continuation of Kay's own print shop, which stood roughly half a mile away in Parliament Close - but its stock of prints, maps and Scottish curiosities makes the name a fitting tribute rather than a coincidence.
source_notes: Historical John Kay biography from Wikipedia/nationalgalleries.org; modern shop details (2017 incorporation, second-hand books, prints/maps) from Edinburgh Council directory and Companies House. Google Places confirms 8 Victoria Street. Checked for duplicate with any existing 'John Kay' POI - none found (no prior entry covers either the historical caricaturist or this shop).

name: India Buildings
address: India Buildings, Victoria Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EX
description: This curved, four-storey Scots Baronial office block was built between 1864 and 1866 to designs by architect David Cousin, its grand interior centred on a domed rotunda ringed by balconies. Its name was likely borrowed from a Liverpool office block of the 1830s, itself named by merchants celebrating the end of the East India Company's monopoly on trade with India - making the building a small piece of Victorian commercial branding transplanted to Edinburgh's Old Town. It originally housed serious institutional tenants, including the British Linen Bank and the Scottish Chamber of Agriculture, fitting for a building built to project financial and civic weight on a street otherwise defined by small shops and closes.
interesting_fact: In January 1906, Indian independence activist Pandurang Mahadev Bapat gave a talk here on British rule in India to an Independent Labour Party meeting - a speech that cost him his government scholarship and pushed him toward the radical movements that led him back to India in 1908 as a freedom fighter.
source_notes: Architectural history from britishlistedbuildings.co.uk and Curious Edinburgh; Bapat anecdote from Curious Edinburgh (curiousedinburgh.org). Google Places confirms location on Victoria Street.

name: George IV Bar
description: The George IV Bar sits midway along George IV Bridge, the elevated street built in 1829-32 to carry traffic clear over the Cowgate far below, connecting the Old Town's South Side to the New Town. Today it's a traditional Scottish public house known for a genuinely serious whisky selection - over 100 different malts and blends - alongside regular live music, making it a quieter, more locals-oriented counterpart to the tourist-heavy pubs down in the Grassmarket and on Victoria Street just below.
interesting_fact: The bridge the bar sits on required demolishing two older Old Town streets, Old Bank Close and Liberton's Wynd, when it was built - meaning the ground beneath the bar's foundations covers what was once part of a completely different, now-vanished street layout.
source_notes: Whisky/live-music details from Tripadvisor/Forever Edinburgh/edinburghguide.com; bridge construction history from georgeivbar.com/history and Wikipedia (George IV Bridge). Google Places confirms 54 George IV Bridge. Kept content focused on the bar itself rather than repeating Victoria Street's existing Thomas Hamilton/Improvement Act history.

name: Augustine United Church
description: Augustine United Church's congregation traces back to 1802, when Reverend John Aikman founded a church nearby, in what is now the site of the National Museum of Scotland, out of Edinburgh's radical Reformation tradition. The current building on George IV Bridge was built between 1857 and 1861 by architects J J & W H Hay, blending Romanesque, Renaissance and Classical detailing beneath a distinctive projecting central tower long nicknamed the 'bride's-cake' tower for its tiered, ornamental profile, restored in 2005. Named for Augustine of Hippo, the church has kept its founding congregation's progressive, community-facing character, today hosting numerous Christian and community organisations rather than functioning as a conventional single-congregation parish church.
interesting_fact: The congregation's roots lie in one of Edinburgh's most deprived districts, where working families and their livestock once lived crowded beneath the wealthy merchants and academics of the Royal Mile above - a history the church still cites as the root of its long-running social and community engagement.
source_notes: History from augustine.org.uk/our-story and nationalchurchestrust.org. Google Places confirms 41 George IV Bridge. Checked against existing George IV Bridge POIs (Elephant House, National Library) - no overlap.

name: Frankenstein & Bier Keller
description: This Gothic former church - built in 1859 and originally an Elim Pentecostal church - now houses one of Edinburgh's more theatrically themed bars. Upstairs, the horror-themed main bar leans into its own name with Frankenstein's-monster decor inside a genuinely Gothic stone shell of pointed arches and spires; downstairs, the Bier Keller recreates a Bavarian beer hall complete with long communal wooden benches, a private bar and a live oompah band on regular nights - an entirely different atmosphere one floor below the horror theming above.
interesting_fact: The building sat abandoned for years after the Elim Pentecostal congregation moved on before its current owners took it on, meaning the pointed arches and spires visible today are the real thing - a genuine former place of worship reused as horror-themed nightlife, not a purpose-built pastiche.
source_notes: Building history (1859, former Elim Pentecostal church) from Historic Environment Scotland listing (LB26862) via Historic Environment Scotland portal; bar/Bier Keller details from tagvenue.com and frankensteinedinburgh.co.uk. Google Places confirms 26 George IV Bridge.

name: Edinburgh Sheriff Court
description: Edinburgh Sheriff Court has a longer institutional history than its current building suggests. Sheriff court business in the city moved through several homes: an 1816 county hall on the corner of Lawnmarket and George IV Bridge, then a purpose-built Renaissance Revival courthouse designed by David Bryce and completed in 1868, before hearings eventually relocated to the Chambers Street building the court occupies today. The office of procurator fiscal that prosecutes cases through this court traces back even further, with the earliest documented references in Scottish records dating to the 1550s - making the basic machinery of local Scottish criminal justice centuries older than any of the buildings that have housed it.
interesting_fact: The Sheriff Court and the adjoining Justice of the Peace Court still share the same ornate iron gateway and postbox-style enquiry point pictured at the entrance, a small formal touch that survives from an era when court buildings were built to visibly project civic authority to everyone passing on the street.
source_notes: Court-building history (1816 county hall, 1868 David Bryce building, later Lawnmarket sheriff court 1934-37) from britishlistedbuildings.co.uk and canmore.org.uk; procurator fiscal origins from Wikipedia (Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service). Google Places confirms current Chambers Street location distinct from the historic Lawnmarket buildings referenced in the history.

name: Crown Office
description: The headquarters of the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service - the body that investigates and prosecutes crime across all of Scotland - occupies a building that started life as a college. Built from 1872-74 to designs by David Rhind (with David Cousin and John Lessels), it was originally the Watt Institution and School of Arts, which in 1885 merged with the centuries-old George Heriot Trust to become Heriot-Watt College, the direct ancestor of today's Heriot-Watt University. Its imposing 268-foot Renaissance-influenced facade, borrowing from French chateau architecture, was designed to give a technical college the civic gravity of a bank or a courthouse - gravity the building has kept ever since, just in service of a different institution.
interesting_fact: Heriot-Watt University's own roots run through this one Chambers Street address before the college eventually outgrew it and moved to its present Riccarton campus, meaning Scotland's chief prosecuting authority now works out of what was, in effect, an early ancestor of a modern Scottish university.
source_notes: Building/institutional history from britishlistedbuildings.co.uk (LB27981) and Heriot-Watt University's own heritage pages. Google Places confirms 25 Chambers Street.

name: Victoria Street's Cobbles
description: The cobbled setts curving down Victoria Street are a genuine survival of a paving technique once universal across Edinburgh's Old Town, laid using roughly cut rectangular granite blocks (properly called 'setts' rather than true rounded cobbles) bedded into sand and gravel. Streets were paved this way from the 18th century onward because granite setts were durable enough to survive horse-drawn cart traffic and could be re-laid individually when damaged, unlike a continuous surface. Most of Edinburgh's other streets have long since been resurfaced in tarmac for modern traffic, making Victoria Street's intact, curving run of setts - still visibly worn smooth by two centuries of footfall and cartwheels - one of the best-preserved and most photographed stretches of historic paving left in the city.
interesting_fact: The double yellow lines painted directly onto the historic setts are a small, constant tension point for conservation bodies - modern traffic regulation applied directly on top of 19th-century stonework, on a street that's otherwise treated as one of Edinburgh's most protected historic assets.
source_notes: General history of granite sett paving as an Edinburgh Old Town convention from established architectural-history knowledge. Google Places confirms Victoria Street location. Kept distinct from the existing Victoria Street POI, which covers the street's own architectural/Diagon Alley history rather than its paving specifically.

name: Quaker Meeting House
address: 7 Victoria Terrace, above, Victoria St, Edinburgh EH1 2JL, UK
description: This Italian Gothic building on Victoria Terrace was built in 1865-66 as a chapel for the United Original Secession Church, then later served as headquarters for the Edinburgh Battalion of the Boys' Brigade. The Religious Society of Friends converted it into Edinburgh's Quaker Meeting House in 1987, giving the city's Quaker community - which had first formed a small central Edinburgh meeting back in 1924 - a permanent, fully accessible home.
interesting_fact: Before settling here, Edinburgh's Central Meeting spent almost fifty years, from 1938 to 1987, gathering in a building on Stafford Street in the New Town.
